questions.challenge_mechanism: The undeflected reading fixes only the ratio E/B1 and not either field on its own, so doubling both fields together leaves the ion's speed, its straight path and its downstream radius completely unchanged, while the time spent in the magnetic region is set by the period 2 pi m/(q B2) and therefore does not respond at all to the speed that the student assumes controls it.
questions.stimulus: A beam of singly ionised atoms of one unknown isotope travels along the axis of a velocity selector. The selector is formed by two parallel plates separated by $d=8.0\ \mathrm{mm}$, with the upper plate at the higher potential and a potential difference $V=288\ \mathrm{V}$ between them; the field between the plates is uniform. The same region contains a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B_{1}=0.60\ \mathrm{T}$, directed perpendicular to both the plates and the beam axis. Ions that emerge along the axis enter a second region, longer than $2R$, that contains only a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B_{2}=0.40\ \mathrm{T}$ directed into the page, with no electric field. Each ion then follows a semicircular path of radius $R=0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ and strikes a detector. Each ion carries charge $+e=+1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$; gravitational and relativistic effects are negligible.

questions.question: The beam enters the selector from the left, travelling along the axis, and the ions are positively charged. The second region is long enough for every ion to complete its semicircular path. Answer all parts using $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ and $1\ \mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the electric field between the plates has magnitude $E=3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, state the direction of $\mathbf{E}$, and determine the direction of $\mathbf{B}_{1}$ for which a positive ion travelling along the axis passes through the selector undeflected. Explain the relationship between the electric and magnetic forces on such an ion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that an ion crosses the selector undeflected only if its speed is $v=\dfrac{E}{B_{1}}$, calculate the value of $v$, and explain why this measurement on its own cannot give the mass of the ion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each ion that leaves the selector enters the second region and moves along a semicircular path of radius $R$ to the detector. Determine the mass of the ion in kilograms and in atomic mass units, and hence state its approximate mass number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The flux density of the selector's magnetic field is now doubled to $B_{1}'=1.20\ \mathrm{T}$, while $E$ and $B_{2}$ are unchanged. Determine the new radius of the semicircular path and the time the ion spends in the second region, and explain why this time is unchanged even though the radius has altered.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The field between parallel plates is uniform, so its magnitude is the potential difference divided by the plate separation:

$$E=\frac{V}{d}=\frac{288}{8.0\times10^{-3}}=3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$$ **(M1)(A1)**

The upper plate is the positive one, so $\mathbf{E}$ is directed vertically downwards, from the upper plate towards the lower plate. **(A1)**

A positive ion travelling along the axis feels an electric force $q\mathbf{E}$ downwards. For it to cross the selector undeflected the magnetic force $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}_{1}$ must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, that is upwards. With $\mathbf{v}$ directed to the right and the required force upwards, the right-hand rule gives $\mathbf{B}_{1}$ directed into the page. **(A1)**

**(b)** Undeflected motion requires the two forces to balance:

$$qE=qvB_{1}$$ **(M1)**

Dividing by $qB_{1}$,

$$v=\frac{E}{B_{1}}$$ **(AG)(A1)**

$$v=\frac{3.6\times10^{4}}{0.60}=6.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ **(A1)**

The balance $qE=qvB_{1}$ contains neither the mass nor the charge of the ion, because both forces are proportional to $q$. The undeflected setting therefore fixes only the speed $v=E/B_{1}$; it carries no information about the mass, and a second measurement that does depend on the mass is needed. **(A1)**

**(c)** In the second region the only force is magnetic, and it provides the centripetal force:

$$qvB_{2}=\frac{mv^{2}}{R}\quad\Rightarrow\quad m=\frac{qB_{2}R}{v}$$ **(M1)(AG)**

$$m=\frac{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.40)(0.15)}{6.0\times10^{4}}=\frac{9.60\times10^{-21}}{6.0\times10^{4}}=1.60\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$$ **(A1)**

Converting with $1\ \mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$,

$$m=\frac{1.60\times10^{-25}}{1.66\times10^{-27}}=96.4\ \mathrm{u}$$ **(A1)**

so the isotope has a mass number of about $96$. **(A1)**

**(d)** If $B_{1}$ is doubled to $1.20\ \mathrm{T}$ while $E$ is unchanged, the transmitted speed becomes

$$v'=\frac{E}{B_{1}'}=\frac{3.6\times10^{4}}{1.20}=3.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ **(M1)**

and the new radius is

$$R'=\frac{mv'}{qB_{2}}=\frac{(1.60\times10^{-25})(3.0\times10^{4})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.40)}=0.075\ \mathrm{m}=\frac{R}{2}$$ **(A1)**

The ion still travels through half a circle, so the time in the second region is half a period:

$$t=\frac{T}{2}=\frac{\pi m}{qB_{2}}=\frac{\pi(1.60\times10^{-25})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.40)}=7.9\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$$ **(A1)**

This is the same as before the change. The period of circular motion in a magnetic field is $2\pi m/(qB_{2})$, which contains no speed, so the ion moves round a smaller semicircle at a proportionally smaller speed and arrives at the detector at exactly the same instant. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for using $E=V/d$ with the separation in metres; a candidate who leaves $d=8.0$ and obtains $36\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ loses the value mark but may still earn the direction marks. The direction of $\mathbf{E}$ must be stated as from the upper (positive) plate to the lower plate. The final (A1) requires the magnetic force to be equal and opposite to the electric force and a right-hand-rule argument; merely writing 'into the page' with no reasoning earns only the direction mark. Accept 'into the paper' or a correct $\otimes$ symbol.

(b) The (AG) requires the balance $qE=qvB_{1}$ to be stated before dividing. The value mark is for $6.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; accept $6.0\times10^{4}$ or $60\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. The final (A1) is for the observation that both forces contain $q$, so the balance is independent of both $q$ and $m$. A candidate who says only 'the mass is not measured' has not explained the insensitivity and forfeits that mark.

(c) Follow-through applies from (b): a candidate whose $v$ is wrong but who uses $m=qB_{2}R/v$ correctly earns the method mark and the conversion mark. Accept $1.6\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and a mass number between $96$ and $97$. Do not accept a mass given without a unit.

(d) The key mark is the last one, for the reason that the period is independent of speed. A candidate who finds the new radius as $R/2$ but claims that the time halves has missed the lever and forfeits that mark. Accept $0.075\ \mathrm{m}$ and $7.9\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$, and accept the time quoted symbolically as $\pi m/(qB_{2})$.
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a measurement that cannot see the fields which produce it. The undeflected condition $qE=qvB_{1}$ fixes the speed as $E/B_{1}$, so the selector responds only to the ratio of the two fields. Doubling $E$ and $B_{1}$ together leaves the speed, the straight path and the downstream radius exactly as they were; there is no reading anywhere in the apparatus that would reveal the change. That is the lever: the quantity the student wants to attribute to a single field is in fact set by a ratio.

The second half of the lever is the time spent in the magnetic region. A candidate who has just seen the radius halve when $B_{1}$ doubles naturally expects the ion to reach the detector in half the time. It does not. The period $T=2\pi m/(qB_{2})$ contains no speed, so the ion crawls round a smaller semicircle at a proportionally smaller speed and arrives at the same instant. This is the same reason a cyclotron can accelerate particles to high energy without the orbit period drifting.

The two unknowns in the problem, the speed and the mass, are deliberately split across two measurements. The selector is sensitive only to $v$; the magnet is sensitive to the product $mv$, and therefore, once $v$ is known, to $m$ alone. Neither reading by itself is enough, and the markscheme rewards the recognition that the selector is blind to mass.

Classic wrong turns: treating the selector balance as $qvB=mv^{2}/r$, which confuses the two regions; forgetting that the electric force is also proportional to $q$ and concluding that the selector measures a charge-to-mass ratio; and using the full period rather than half a period for a semicircular path. A useful sanity check is dimensional: $E/B_{1}$ has units of $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $qB_{2}R/v$ has units of kilograms.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the D.2 and D.3 bullets on uniform fields, forces on charges and the motion of a charged particle in crossed and magnetic fields. The design was constructed backwards from two levers: the undeflected condition fixes only the ratio $E/B_{1}$, so the apparatus is blind to a common scaling of the two fields, and the semicircle time depends only on $m$, $q$ and $B_{2}$. The values $d=8.0\ \mathrm{mm}$, $V=288\ \mathrm{V}$, $B_{1}=0.60\ \mathrm{T}$, $B_{2}=0.40\ \mathrm{T}$ and $R=0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ were chosen so that $E=3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $v=6.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $m=1.60\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$ (mass number $96$) and $T/2=7.9\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$ all come out cleanly, and so that doubling $B_{1}$ gives exactly $R/2$. The item is not a reskin of any existing one: the bank's D.4 item is about motional emf and terminal speed, and its D.1 item is about orbital transfers.

verification.method: Electric field from E = V/d = 288/8.0e-3 = 3.6e4 V/m; transmitted speed from v = E/B1 = 6.0e4 m/s; ion mass from m = q B2 R / v = 1.60e-25 kg = 96.4 u; period T = 2 pi m/(q B2) = 1.5708e-5 s so the semicircle time is 7.854e-6 s; after doubling B1 the speed is 3.0e4 m/s, the radius is 0.075 m and the semicircle time is unchanged. The scaled-field case was re-checked by confirming that 2E/(2B1) = E/B1.

questions.title: The work function that cancels in the difference
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: E.1 Structure of the atom and E.2 Quantum physics (AHL): energy levels of a hydrogen-like ion E_n = -A/n^2, spectral lines from transitions between levels, ionisation energy and its scaling with Z^2, the photoelectric effect, the photoelectric equation eV_s = hf - phi, stopping voltage and work function
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: E.1 Structure of the atom / E.2 Quantum physics
questions.challenge_mechanism: Each stopping voltage is an aggregate of the photon energy and the work function, so one reading gives a single equation in two unknowns and cannot be solved; only the difference of the two stopping voltages makes the work function cancel and exposes the energy-level scale A, after which the work function is recovered from either reading.
questions.stimulus:
A discharge tube contains a gas of a hydrogen-like ion, that is, an ion with a single electron and nuclear charge number $Z$. The energy levels of the ion are $E_{n}=-\dfrac{A}{n^{2}}$, where $A$ is a positive constant and $n$ is the principal quantum number. The light emitted by the tube is passed through a monochromator, and two spectral lines are isolated in turn and directed at the same metal photocathode inside an evacuated photocell. The two lines are identified as the $n=4\to2$ and $n=2\to1$ transitions of the ion, and the stopping voltage is measured for each.

| Spectral line | Stopping voltage |
|---|---|
| $n=4\to2$ | $5.7\ \mathrm{V}$ |
| $n=2\to1$ | $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$ |

The work function of the cathode is $\phi$ and the electron charge is $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$.

figure.caption: Energy-level diagram of the hydrogen-like ion, showing the two transitions whose emitted lines are used in the photocell. The level spacing scales with the constant A.

questions.question: Assume that the light from each line is monochromatic and that the photocell is ideal, so that the stopping voltage corresponds to the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons. The values of the Planck constant and the speed of light are not needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the stopping voltage measures the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, and state the photoelectric equation that relates the stopping voltage, the photon energy and the work function of the cathode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the photon energies of the $n=4\to2$ and $n=2\to1$ transitions of this ion are $\dfrac{3A}{16}$ and $\dfrac{3A}{4}$ respectively, and state which of the two measured stopping voltages corresponds to each transition.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the two measured stopping voltages, determine the value of $A$ and the work function $\phi$ of the cathode, and explain why neither stopping voltage on its own is sufficient to find $\phi$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the nuclear charge number $Z$ of the ion and its ionisation energy in electronvolts, and explain how the wavelengths of the two spectral lines would change if the gas were replaced by a hydrogen-like ion of larger $Z$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The emitted photoelectrons have a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum $K_{\max}$. **(A1)** The stopping voltage is the reverse potential difference that just reduces the photocurrent to zero, so it removes the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons: $eV_{s}=K_{\max}$. **(A1)** Energy conservation for the absorption of a single photon gives $hf=\phi+K_{\max}$, and therefore

$$eV_{s}=hf-\phi$$ **(A1)**

**(b)** The energy of the photon emitted in a transition equals the difference between the two levels involved. **(M1)** For $n=4\to2$,

$$hf_{1}=E_{4}-E_{2}=-\frac{A}{16}-\left(-\frac{A}{4}\right)=\frac{A}{4}-\frac{A}{16}=\frac{3A}{16}$$ **(A1)**

and for $n=2\to1$,

$$hf_{2}=E_{2}-E_{1}=-\frac{A}{4}-(-A)=A-\frac{A}{4}=\frac{3A}{4}$$ **(A1)**

Since $\dfrac{3A}{4}>\dfrac{3A}{16}$, the $n=2\to1$ line delivers the more energetic photons and must give the larger stopping voltage, $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$; the $n=4\to2$ line corresponds to $5.7\ \mathrm{V}$. **(A1)**

**(c)** Applying $eV_{s}=E_{\text{photon}}-\phi$ to each line, and working in electronvolts so that the stopping voltage in volts is numerically equal to the kinetic energy in electronvolts:

$$e(5.7)=\frac{3A}{16}-\phi \qquad\text{and}\qquad e(36.3)=\frac{3A}{4}-\phi$$ **(M1)**

Subtracting the first equation from the second eliminates $\phi$:

$$e(36.3-5.7)=\frac{3A}{4}-\frac{3A}{16}=\frac{12A-3A}{16}=\frac{9A}{16}$$ **(M1)(A1)**

$$A=\frac{16\times 30.6}{9}=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$$ **(A1)**

Substituting this back into the first equation gives the work function:

$$\phi=\frac{3A}{16}-e(5.7)=\frac{3(54.4)}{16}-5.7=10.2-5.7=4.5\ \mathrm{eV}$$ **(A1)**

Each stopping voltage is the difference between a photon energy and the work function. A single reading is therefore one equation in two unknowns, $A$ and $\phi$, and cannot be solved; only the difference of the two readings removes $\phi$ and fixes $A$, after which $\phi$ follows from either line. **(A1)**

**(d)** For a hydrogen-like ion the energy-level constant is

$$A=13.6Z^{2}\ \mathrm{eV}$$ **(M1)**

so

$$Z^{2}=\frac{A}{13.6}=\frac{54.4}{13.6}=4.0\quad\Rightarrow\quad Z=2$$ **(A1)**

The ion is therefore $\mathrm{He}^{+}$, and its ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the electron from $n=1$ to $E=0$, namely $A=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$. **(A1)** Because $A\propto Z^{2}$, a larger $Z$ increases every transition energy. Since $E=hc/\lambda$, each wavelength would be shorter, so both lines would shift to shorter wavelengths, giving more energetic photons and larger stopping voltages. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The first (A1) is for the statement that the photoelectrons have a maximum kinetic energy; the second for $eV_{s}=K_{\max}$; the third for the full energy balance $eV_{s}=hf-\phi$. A candidate who writes $eV_{s}=hf+\phi$ has the sign of the work function wrong and loses the final mark. Accept 'stopping potential' for 'stopping voltage'.

(b) The (M1) is for the principle that a photon's energy equals the difference between the two levels involved. The two (A1)s are for the algebraic results $3A/16$ and $3A/4$. The final (A1) requires both the identification and a reason: because $3A/4>3A/16$, the $n=2\to1$ line gives the larger stopping voltage, $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$. A candidate who reverses the correspondence has made a physics error rather than an arithmetic slip and loses that mark.

(c) The first (M1) is for writing the two photoelectric equations, one for each line. The second (M1) is for subtracting them so that $\phi$ cancels; a candidate who substitutes one equation into the other will still reach the answer but should be given the method mark only if the algebra is shown. Accept $A$ between $54$ and $54.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\phi$ between $4.4$ and $4.6\ \mathrm{eV}$. Follow-through applies: a candidate whose $A$ is slightly off but whose $\phi$ is consistent with it keeps the final mark.

(d) The (M1) is for quoting or deriving $A=13.6Z^{2}\ \mathrm{eV}$. Accept $Z=2$ with the identification of the ion as $\mathrm{He}^{+}$. The final mark requires the direction of the shift: shorter wavelengths, larger photon energies. 'The lines would move' with no direction earns nothing.
questions.explanation:
The difficulty here is not the photoelectric equation, which most candidates can quote, but the fact that a single stopping voltage is an aggregate. It is the photon energy minus the work function, and both are unknown, so one reading gives one equation in two unknowns and is unsolvable. Candidates who have practised only single-line problems will look for a way to pin the work function directly and will not find one; the question is designed so that the only route is to take a difference.

The difference works because the work function appears in both equations with the same sign and the same magnitude. Subtracting removes it exactly, leaving the difference of the two photon energies, which is a pure property of the ion. This is the same trick used in the Millikan experiment to extract the Planck constant from the slope of a stopping-voltage against frequency graph: the intercept carries the work function and the slope carries $h/e$, so a single point cannot separate them. Here the two transitions play the role of two frequencies.

The ion is deliberately left unnamed. The student must recognise that the level spacing of a hydrogen-like ion scales as $Z^{2}$, so recovering $A$ is equivalent to recovering $Z$, and $A=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$ identifies $\mathrm{He}^{+}$. The two chosen lines, $n=4\to2$ and $n=2\to1$, were picked so that their photon-energy difference is exactly $9A/16$, which makes the arithmetic clean; the ratio of their photon energies, $4:1$, is also a useful check.

Classic wrong turns: assuming that the stopping voltage equals the photon energy, which ignores the work function entirely; trying to find the two wavelengths from the same two equations, which is circular because the wavelengths are what the transition energies already determine; and treating the ion as hydrogen, so that $A=13.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is inconsistent with the measured stopping voltages. The last error is easy to make, because the $n=2\to1$ line of hydrogen would give a stopping voltage near $9.1\ \mathrm{V}$, far from the $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$ measured, and a quick numerical check catches it.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the E.1 and E.2 bullets on hydrogen-like energy levels and the photoelectric effect. The design pairs two spectral lines with two stopping voltages so that the work function cancels in the difference and the energy-level constant $A$ is exposed; this is the two-unknowns-from-two-aggregate-readings lever, and the question is built backwards from that cancellation rather than from a template. The values were chosen so that the photon energies are $10.2\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $40.8\ \mathrm{eV}$, the stopping voltages $5.7\ \mathrm{V}$ and $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$, $A=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\phi=4.5\ \mathrm{eV}$, with $Z=2$ identifying $\mathrm{He}^{+}$. The combination of a spectral-energy-level recovery with a photoelectric measurement is not present in the bank, and the item is not a reskin of the bank's E.3 two-isotope decay question.

verification.method: Photon energies from the level differences 3A/16 and 3A/4; the two photoelectric equations subtracted to give A = 16(36.3-5.7)/9 = 54.4 eV, then phi = 3A/16 - 5.7 = 4.5 eV; the reverse substitution 3A/4 - phi = 36.3 V was checked; Z from A = 13.6 Z^2 gives Z = 2 and the ionisation energy equals A = 54.4 eV.
